title: Borrowing Arrows with Straw Boats: Not Zhuge Liang? Who Nearly Capsized in 38 Characters
description:
You've surely heard of the straw boats that borrowed arrows: a thick fog, twenty straw boats, 100,000 arrows. But in more than a thousand years, three different men have stood at the bow for that one turn.

This episode follows that turn backwards. Chapter 46 of today's standard edition of Romance of the Three Kingdoms has 5,000-6,000 arrows per boat and more than 100,000 carried ashore. In the Jiajing edition, with its preface dated 1522, Zhuge Liang says "100,000-odd", but the count ashore is "over 90,000", and the section is titled "Zhuge Liang Outwits Zhou Yu". In the Yuan-dynasty Sanguozhi Pinghua (c. 1321-1323), the man who turns his boat to receive arrows before Red Cliffs and shouts "Chancellor, thanks for the arrows!" is Zhou Yu. Further back, Pei Songzhi's note to the Ruxu entry for Jian'an 18 (213) in the Records of the Three Kingdoms (Annals of Sun Quan) quotes the Weilüe: Sun Quan sails a big ship to view Cao Cao's camp, it takes so many arrows it nearly capsizes, and he turns it to receive arrows on the other side; "the arrows even, the ship level, he went back". Those 38 characters have no fog, no straw, no numbers and no thanks. The same note quotes the Wu Li, which says Cao Cao ordered that "bows and crossbows must not shoot at will" and that Sun Quan rode a light boat. Pei Songzhi copied both. Sima Guang's Zizhi Tongjian keeps neither account of Ruxu and gives no reason; chapter 61 of the Romance also covers Ruxu, with no arrow-struck ship. That year Zhuge Liang and Guan Yu were holding Jingzhou, and Zhou Yu had died in 210. The earliest record we have found of a boat turned to receive arrows is Sun Quan's ship at Ruxu, and only one book, the Weilüe, says so: filed.

The official history and the Zizhi Tongjian follow the Daizhige transcriptions (from the Siku Quanshu edition), the Pinghua the Daizhige transcription, the Jiajing edition the Wikisource transcription (not checked against scans), and the standard edition Project Gutenberg; we did not check the Jin and Yuan Three Kingdoms plays. Sources are listed in the references below; sentences that begin "we think" are the channel's view.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant to resemble anyone.

Information as of 2026-10-20 (rewritten on 2026-10-25 under new guidelines)

chapters.teller-stage: A Yuan tale turns the boat
chapters.arc-note: 213 AD: a big ship at Ruxu

cj101.text: You've heard of the straw boats that borrowed arrows: fog, 20 straw boats, 100,000 arrows.

cj102.text: But for that one turn, three men have stood at the bow in over 1,000 years.

cj103.text: The novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms: night three, 20 straw boats enter the Yangtze fog.

cj104.text: Cao's men shoot blindly; suddenly the boats turn to receive arrows on the other side.

cj105.text: As the fog clears, the crews shout: "Thanks for the arrows, Chancellor!"

cj106.text: But the Records of the Three Kingdoms, notes and all, has no "borrow arrows."

cj107.text: Odder still: in a 700-year-old storyteller's text, a different man shouts the thanks.

cj108.text: Over 1,000 years earlier, a book has a big ship nearly capsized by arrows.

cj109.text: This file traces that one turn from the novel back 1,800 years.

cj110.text: Straw boats: not Zhuge Liang after all?

cj201.text: In today's standard edition, it is: chapter 46 is "Kongming Borrows Arrows by a Clever Plan."

cj202.text: In the story, Zhou Yu is alarmed and says: "This man must not be allowed to live."

cj203.text: Needing a plausible excuse to be rid of him, he asks Zhuge Liang to make those 100,000 arrows in ten days.

cj204.text: But Zhuge Liang says Cao is near; ten days is too late, three will do;

cj205.text: he even signs a pledge to be punished if he fails.

cj206.text: Three days, all those arrows. Where would you find materials?

cj207.text: Zhou Yu even has the craftsmen stall and short him on materials.

cj208.text: Those 20 straw boats came from Lu Su in secret, with just 30 men each.

cj210.text: The novel says he had predicted that fog three days before.

cj211.text: The novel even pauses here for a rhapsody, "Great Fog over the River," all about the fog.

cj212.text: Bows west, sterns east, in a line, they drum and shout in the fog.

cj213.text: That arrow rain: Cao fears an ambush in the fog, so he adds over 10,000 archers from land camps.

cj214.text: One side full, Zhuge Liang turns the boats bows east and closes in for more arrows.

cj215.text: Three days later, how many did Zhuge Liang hand in?

cj216.text: The standard edition: about 5,000-6,000 per boat; carried ashore, more than 100,000.

cj217.text: Zhuge Liang adds: "It cost Jiangdong no effort at all."

cj218.text: Zhou Yu sighs: "I can't match him."

cj219.text: As a kid, I too found it the cleverest scene in the Three Kingdoms.

cj220.text: Yet the earliest Ming edition has other numbers.

cj221.text: It's the Jiajing-era edition, which opens with a preface dated 1522.

cj223.text: but what's carried ashore to the command tent is just over 90,000.

cj224.text: In one passage, the novel's two numbers clash.

cj225.text: Oddly, in this edition the section is titled "Zhuge Liang Outwits Zhou Yu,"

cj226.text: the volume never says "borrow arrows"; the standard edition's title adds it.

cj227.text: But did anyone write that turn before this novel?

cj301.text: Yes. The 700-year-old storyteller's text I mentioned: the Yuan-era Sanguozhi Pinghua.

cj302.text: Remember, someone else shouts the thanks: the man at the bow is Zhou Yu.

cj303.text: Before Red Cliffs, after a shouting match, Zhou Yu sails out with a big ship and ten small,

cj304.text: and Cao's camp sets thousands of men shooting.

cj305.text: Left side full, he turns the boat so the right receives arrows.

cj306.text: Surprisingly, the boats soon bristle with arrows; the Pinghua says several million.

cj307.text: Listen to that number: millions. The novel's later figure seems modest by comparison.

cj308.text: Zhou Yu cheers: "Chancellor, thanks for the arrows!"

cj309.text: Cao Cao fumes: "Fight tomorrow and take the arrows back!"

cj310.text: No fog here, no straw bundles; the boats hang curtains. And no three-day deadline.

cj311.text: The tale is a battle; Zhou Yu isn't out to swindle arrows.

cj313.text: He appears early, even asking Zhou Yu in person to fight;

cj314.text: but he has no part in the arrow scene.

cj315.text: In versions we can find, only the Ming novel gives Zhuge Liang this scene.

cj316.text: Jin and Yuan stages had 30-plus Three Kingdoms plays; we opened none, hence only "versions we can find."

cj317.text: But before the Pinghua, did anyone write of a boat turning to receive arrows?

cj401.text: Yes, in the notes to a history: the first month of Jian'an 18, 213 AD, at the mouth of the Ruxu.

cj402.text: A year earlier, on Lü Meng's advice, Sun Quan fortified the Ruxu mouth and held it.

cj403.text: The generals balked: fight ashore, wash your feet, reboard. Why a fort? Sun Quan approved; it was built.

cj404.text: Cao Cao set out last October; they stalled here for over a month.

cj405.text: By then, Red Cliffs was five years in the past.

cj407.text: Chen Shou's text says only: Cao saw Sun's orderly army, sighed, and pulled back.

cj408.text: Cao's chapter: he took Sun's camp west of the river, seized a commander, then withdrew.

cj409.text: Neither has arrows or a boat. So where are the arrows?

cj410.text: In notes Pei Songzhi added 200-plus years later;

cj411.text: he copied in what Chen Shou left out, from other books.

cj412.text: Under this line he quotes the Weilüe: written by Yu Huan of Wei back then, now lost.

cj413.text: No book is quoted more across Pei's notes; today we know it only from the pieces he copied.

cj414.text: Sun Quan sails a big ship to see Cao's camp; Cao has archers shoot wildly; arrows stud it.

cj415.text: One side too heavy, it nearly capsizes: that's the big ship I mentioned.

cj417.text: He turns it to receive arrows on the other side; arrows even, it levels, and he leaves.

cj418.text: Back here, the turn from the opening was to avoid capsizing.

cj419.text: Remember: no "borrow arrows," even in the notes?

cj420.text: Look at the word used: not "borrow" but "receive." Receive arrows.

cj421.text: But this passage is just 38 characters.

cj422.text: No fog, no straw, no numbers, and no one says thanks.

cj423.text: In the whole Records, notes included, "receive arrows" appears only here.

cj424.text: Receiving arrows is passive; nor does the text say he kept them.

cj426.text: No proof; we can only say the move is the same.

cj427.text: We think it looks more like a scramble not to capsize than a clever plan.

cj428.text: Some now call it the "prototype" of the straw boats; we'd only say it's the closest real event.

cj429.text: In the same note, right beside it, Pei Songzhi copied another book.

cj501.text: It's the Wu Li, by Hu Chong of Wu, Prefect of the Secretariat when Wu fell.

cj502.text: It says Sun Quan challenged Cao several times, but Cao stayed put; so Sun sailed up to Cao's camp himself.

cj503.text: Cao's generals think it's a challenge and want to charge; Cao says, "Sun Quan wants to see my army himself."

cj504.text: He orders: hold ranks, no shooting at will.

cj505.text: No shooting. First time, I flipped back to the Weilüe, thinking I'd missed something.

cj506.text: And here, Sun Quan rides not a big ship but a light boat.

cj507.text: Strangely, this boat turns too: after five or six li, it turns back, with music playing all the way.

cj508.text: Seeing his orderly fleet, Cao sighs: "A son should be like Sun Zhongmou."

cj509.text: You've heard that line; fewer quote the rest: "Liu Jingsheng's sons are mere pigs and dogs."

cj510.text: Cao, saying this, was nearly 60; Sun Quan was just past 30.

cj511.text: Both books tell of the same visit by Sun in person;

cj512.text: the wild volley in one becomes no shooting in the other.

cj513.text: And the two authors came from the two warring sides.

cj514.text: You're the editor: a Wei man says they shot, a Wu man says they didn't. Which stays?

cj515.text: Why didn't Pei Songzhi pick one?

cj516.text: In Yuanjia 6, that is 429, he gave his notes to the emperor;

cj517.text: his memorial states the rule: where accounts differ and can't be judged, copy all in for the record.

cj518.text: Elsewhere he even criticized Hu Chong, calling his book eccentric;

cj519.text: yet in this note he copies both, without a word of comment.

cj520.text: So which side did later historians believe?

cj601.text: Later, writing Ruxu into his Zizhi Tongjian, Sima Guang

cj603.text: and Sun's letter to Cao: "Spring waters are rising; you had best leave soon."

cj604.text: Another sheet said: "While you live, I can't rest easy." Cao read it, said Sun Quan hadn't lied to him, and withdrew.

cj605.text: He left out the Weilüe's arrow ship;

cj606.text: and the Wu Li's light boat and order as well.

cj608.text: Read only the Zizhi Tongjian and you'd never know this ship was at Ruxu.

cj609.text: Better still is the novel itself. In chapter 61, Romance of the Three Kingdoms covers Ruxu too:

cj610.text: The sigh is there, the letter too, and Sun Quan's big ship; yet no arrows are received.

cj611.text: Instead, in that chapter, Sun's ambushers lead 3,000 archers to shoot wildly at Cao: the reverse.

cj612.text: It looks as if the novel moved that ship out of Ruxu and into chapter 46.

cj613.text: I say "looks as if" because there's no direct proof.

cj614.text: Whoever moved it, the novel has Zhuge Liang at the bow.

cj615.text: But in the first month of 213, where was Zhuge Liang himself?

cj701.text: He and Guan Yu were guarding Jingzhou; that month, he wasn't at Ruxu.

cj702.text: He was 33; his lord Liu Bei took tens of thousands of infantry to Yizhou.

cj703.text: Sun Quan sought aid; Liu Bei used it to ask Liu Zhang for 10,000 men, getting 4,000, half the rest.

cj704.text: Sun's ally, busy with plans in Sichuan, never came.

cj705.text: And his famous Red Cliffs? In the histories, what did he do in that battle?

cj706.text: Per the history, Zhou Yu's officer Huang Gai set the fire:

cj707.text: dozens of ships of wood and straw doused in oil; first a fake surrender letter, then fire.

cj708.text: Notice? In the history, Red Cliffs' straw was for burning, not for catching arrows.

cj709.text: Zhuge Liang was the alliance envoy: with Liu Bei at Xiakou, he urged haste and asked to see Sun Quan.

cj710.text: Deal done, Sun sent Zhou Yu, Cheng Pu, Lu Su and 30,000 marines back with him.

cj712.text: Three years before, he'd died of illness at Baqiu, aged 36.

cj713.text: I said three men have stood at the bow for that turn: the novel's Zhuge Liang, the Pinghua's Zhou Yu, and the notes' Sun Quan.

cj714.text: So we file this: the earliest record we've found of the straw boats' turn

cj715.text: is not on Zhuge Liang's boat, but on Sun Quan's.

cj716.text: In your version, who's at the bow? Let me know below.

cj717.text: Only what's on record here. Subscribe to open the files together.
